title: Recovery, Minus One Detail
blurb: Six BCP/DR vocabulary pairs examiners love to swap for each other. One flipped detail — a metric, a site's readiness, a backup's chain — tells them apart every time.
source: Chapple CISSP SG 10ed ch.18 · outline 7.10 (Implement recovery strategies), 7.11 (Implement DR processes)

pairs.dimension: time to restore vs data you can afford to lose

a.text: The DR plan sets a four-hour ceiling on how long the claims-processing system may stay unavailable after a declared disaster.
a.why: It caps clock time down — restoration speed — and says nothing about how much data may be lost, which is the other measurement's job.

b.text: The DR plan sets a four-hour ceiling on how much claims data may be lost, measured backward from the moment the system fails.
b.why: It caps data loss measured backward from failure, not downtime — the same four-hour figure now describes lost records, not how long the system stays down.

pairs.dimension: data the function may lose vs downtime the function may survive

a.text: The BIA records that order-entry may lose at most two days of captured orders in a failure, counted backward from the moment it stops.
a.why: Counting backward from the failure to fix how stale the recovered records may be is a data-currency ceiling, saying nothing about how long the function may sit idle.

b.text: The BIA records that order-entry may sit unavailable for at most two days after a failure before the business can no longer survive the outage.
b.why: The same two-day figure now measures forward from the failure as the outer downtime the business can absorb — the ceiling every recovery-time target for the function must fit inside.

pairs.dimension: data already current vs data still needs restoring

a.text: The brokerage's leased failover facility continuously mirrors live trade data, so operations can shift over within minutes of a declared disaster.
a.why: Continuously current data plus near-instant takeover is the marker — the other facility type has the hardware ready but not the live data, so it can't cut over this fast.

b.text: The brokerage's leased failover facility has racks and network drops preinstalled, but last night's trade data still has to be loaded before operations can shift over, a process expected to take about half a day.
b.why: Hardware present but data not yet current, needing restoration work before cutover, is the marker — the other facility type would already hold live, replicated data.

pairs.dimension: some equipment preinstalled vs no computing facilities installed

a.text: The utility's alternate facility already has servers and network gear racked and ready, needing only current data loaded before staff can resume billing operations.
a.why: Preinstalled hardware and connectivity awaiting only current data is the marker — the other facility type has no computing equipment installed at all yet.

b.text: The utility's alternate facility is an empty shell with power and HVAC provisioned, but no servers, network gear, or computing equipment of any kind installed.
b.why: No preinstalled computing facilities at all, only the building shell and utilities, is the marker — the other facility type already has hardware racked and waiting on data.

pairs.dimension: captures everything every run vs captures changes since the last full run

a.text: Every Sunday night, the archive job copies the entire file server's contents regardless of which files changed that week, resetting every archive bit.
a.why: Copying everything unconditionally and clearing every archive bit each run is the marker — the other scheme would only capture what changed since the last full run.

b.text: Every weeknight, the archive job copies only the files changed since Sunday's full backup without touching the archive bit, so Thursday's job is visibly larger than Monday's.
b.why: Growing nightly size, because it always measures from the last full backup and never clears the archive bit, is the marker — a full run would instead copy everything, every night.

pairs.dimension: chains off the last backup of any type vs always measures from the last full

a.text: Restoring the crashed file server needs Monday's full backup plus every single nightly job run since, replayed in order.
a.why: A multi-step restore chain, needing the full plus every backup since in sequence, is the marker — each job only captured changes since the last job of any type, whichever that was.

b.text: Restoring the crashed file server needs only Monday's full backup and last night's job, nothing else, no matter how many nights have passed since.
b.why: A two-job restore, the last full plus just the most recent run, is the marker — the other scheme would instead require replaying every night's job since the full.
